Reentrancy lets an attacker slip back into a contract before its state finishes updating.

An external call transfers control to the called contract, which may call back into the original function.

Reentrancy is not limited to Ether transfers; any call to another contract can create a re-entry path.

Mitigate by updating state before external calls and, if needed, adding a reentrancy guard; also examine cross-function paths.

Can you verify that every external interaction in your code follows the checks-effects-interactions order?

Missing access control lets an unintended account call privileged functions.

Permissions are missing or applied inconsistently across privileged entry points, creating the gap.

Different privileged operations can require different roles.

Mitigate by defining roles explicitly and testing unauthorized calls for every privileged operation.

How will you verify that role assignment and removal, which are permission-sensitive operations, are correctly restricted?

If your contract trusts a price feed without resistance, a low-liquidity pool can be manipulated and stale data may be used. Have you verified feed liquidity and timestamps? DM to discuss a security review.
Using tx.origin for auth lets a malicious intermediary contract trick a victim into authorizing actions. Have you checked caller-based checks on all call paths? DM to discuss a security review.
Can a loop over growing on-chain data exceed the gas limit? Unbounded iteration can grow work without bound, eventually stalling the contract. DM to discuss a security review.
